questions.topic_aspect: Angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference
questions.mark_scheme:
M1 for recognising that the angle at the centre (120°) is twice the angle at the circumference (or dividing 120 by 2)
A1 for $x = 60^\circ$
questions.misconception_targeted: Confusing which angle is 'at the centre' vs 'at the circumference'

questions.topic_aspect: Angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees
questions.mark_scheme:
M1 for recognising that angle $PQR = 90^\circ$ since $PR$ is a diameter (angle in a semicircle is $90^\circ$), and using angle sum of triangle $PQR = 180^\circ$: $x = 180 - 90 - 35$
A1 for $x = 55^\circ$ (with correct reason: angle in a semicircle is $90^\circ$)
questions.misconception_targeted: Not recognising the diameter as the key feature triggering this theorem

questions.topic_aspect: Angles in the same segment are equal
questions.mark_scheme:
M1 for identifying that angle ACB and angle ADB are subtended by the same chord (AB) and lie in the same segment (on the same side of AB)
A1 for stating the reason: angles in the same segment (subtended by the same arc) are equal
A1 for $x = 38^\circ$

Note: award full marks only if reasoning references "same segment" / "same arc" - a bare numerical answer of 38 with no reasoning scores M0A0A1 (1 mark only) since the reason was explicitly requested.
questions.misconception_targeted: Assuming all angles in a circle are equal regardless of segment

questions.topic_aspect: Cyclic quadrilaterals — opposite angles sum to 180 degrees
questions.correct_answer: x = 34; Angle A = 68 degrees; Angle C = 112 degrees
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) M1 for use of opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180 degrees, i.e. 2x + 3x + 10 = 180
A1 for x = 34
(b) M1 (ft) for substituting their value of x into both expressions: angle A = 2(34) = 68 degrees, angle C = 3(34)+10 = 112 degrees
A1 for correct angle A = 68 degrees AND correct angle C = 112 degrees (with a check that 68 + 112 = 180)
Note: Award 0 marks in part (a) if student assumes opposite angles are equal (2x = 3x+10) as this reflects the targeted misconception; no ft marks available from an incorrect equal-angles method in part (b) either.
questions.misconception_targeted: Thinking opposite angles are equal rather than supplementary

questions.topic_aspect: Tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius; tangent-radius properties applied in context
questions.mark_scheme:
M1 for recognising that angle $OTP = 90^\circ$ (tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact)
A1 for stating angle $OTP = 90^\circ$ correctly with reason (tangent/radius property)
M1 for using angle sum of triangle $OTP$: $x + 90 + 24 = 180$
A1 for correct answer $x = 66^\circ$ with reason (angles in a triangle sum to $180^\circ$)

Note: full marks require correct reasons stated; correct answer with no reasons scores maximum 2 marks (M1 A0 M1 A0 equivalent — award M marks for correct method only, reasons required for A marks).
questions.misconception_targeted: Forgetting the right angle formed between tangent and radius

questions.correct_answer: (a) $x = 72^\circ$ (angle in alternate segment equals angle between tangent and chord). (b) Angle $ABD = 180 - 72 - 53 = 55^\circ$; since the three angles $72^\circ$, $53^\circ$, $55^\circ$ are all different, no two sides of triangle $ABD$ are equal, so it is not isosceles.
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) M1 for identifying that angle DAB is in the alternate segment to the tangent-chord angle SDB (correctly matching the 72° angle with its correct alternate segment, not the wrong segment on the other side of DB); A1 for $x = 72^\circ$ with correct reason stated (alternate segment theorem).
(b) M1 for using angle sum of triangle ABD: angle ABD $= 180 - 72 - 53 = 55^\circ$; A1 for correct conclusion that since all three angles (72°, 53°, 55°) are different, all three sides are different lengths, so triangle ABD is not isosceles.
questions.misconception_targeted: Matching the wrong angle to the wrong segment when applying the theorem

questions.topic_aspect: Multi-step problem combining cyclic quadrilateral, tangent-radius properties, and isosceles triangles formed by two radii
questions.correct_answer:
(a) Angle OBD = 16 degrees, since OB = OD (both radii), triangle OBD is isosceles, so base angles OBD and ODB are equal: (180 - 148)/2 = 16 degrees.
(b) Angle BCD = 146 degrees
questions.misconception_targeted: Not identifying isosceles triangles formed by two radii, leading to incorrect angle assumptions
